name: GPON Fiber to the Home
speed: Up to 2.5 Gbps down / 1.25 Gbps up
bestFor: Homes in towns and along existing fiber routes
description: Gigabit Passive Optical Network (GPON) splits one fiber from the provider's office into as many as 64 homes using passive optical splitters. Because nothing between the office and the home needs power, it is reliable and inexpensive to maintain once built.

name: XGS-PON Fiber
description: XGS-PON is the next generation of passive optical networking. It runs on the same fiber as GPON but uses different wavelengths, so providers can upgrade customers to 10 Gbps without digging new trenches.

name: Active Ethernet Fiber
bestFor: Remote farms, towers, and large businesses
description: Active Ethernet gives each customer a dedicated fiber strand straight to a powered switch. It reaches much farther than PON, which makes it useful for connecting distant customers and cell towers.

name: CBRS Fixed Wireless
bestFor: Rural homes within a few miles of a tower
description: Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) uses the 3.55–3.7 GHz band in the United States. A spectrum access system coordinates who can transmit, giving rural providers access to high-quality spectrum without buying an expensive license.

name: Next-Generation Fixed Wireless
bestFor: Wooded or hilly areas where fiber is too costly
description: New fixed wireless platforms use advanced antennas and interference cancellation to deliver near-fiber speeds even without a clear view of the tower. They let rural providers reach homes behind trees and hills.

name: Unlicensed 5 GHz Fixed Wireless
bestFor: Low-cost service in open, flat terrain
description: Many small rural internet providers use 5 GHz radios that need no license. Equipment is affordable, but the band is shared with other users, so performance can drop when interference is high.

name: 60 GHz Millimeter Wave
bestFor: Small towns and neighborhoods with short distances
description: 60 GHz radios carry huge amounts of data over very short links. Oxygen absorbs the signal quickly, so links are short, but that same property means little interference between neighbors.

name: TV White Space
bestFor: Remote areas with heavy trees or hills
description: TV white space uses unused television channels in the UHF band. These low frequencies travel through foliage and over hills, but the narrow channels limit speed.

name: Licensed Microwave Backhaul
bestFor: Connecting rural towers to the internet
description: Licensed point-to-point microwave links in the 6–23 GHz bands carry traffic from tower to tower. The license protects the link from interference, so it is the backbone of many rural wireless networks.

name: E-Band Microwave
description: E-band links use the 70/80 GHz bands to move multi-gigabit traffic across short distances. Heavy rain can reduce range, so engineers plan link distances around local rainfall.

name: Low-Earth-Orbit Satellite
bestFor: Very remote homes with no other options
description: Low-Earth-orbit (LEO) constellations use thousands of satellites flying about 550 km above Earth. Being so close greatly reduces latency compared with older satellites, making video calls and gaming possible.

name: Geostationary Satellite
lineOfSight: Clear view of the southern sky
bestFor: Basic browsing and email in isolated areas
description: Geostationary satellites orbit about 35,786 km above the equator and appear fixed in the sky. The long distance causes high latency, which makes real-time applications difficult.

name: 4G LTE Home Internet
bestFor: Light users near an existing cell tower
description: 4G LTE home internet uses a cellular router inside the home. It is easy to install, but speeds depend on how many people share the same tower.

name: 5G Home Internet
bestFor: Homes on the edge of towns with 5G coverage
description: 5G home internet uses mid-band spectrum to deliver faster speeds than 4G. Rural 5G coverage is still growing, so availability varies widely by location.

name: VDSL2 Copper
bestFor: Homes close to a telephone company cabinet
description: VDSL2 sends broadband over existing telephone wires. Speeds drop quickly with distance, so it works best when a fiber-fed cabinet is nearby.

name: ADSL2+ Copper
bestFor: Basic service on existing phone lines
description: ADSL2+ is an older form of DSL still found in many rural areas. It reaches farther than VDSL2, but its speeds no longer meet modern broadband definitions.

name: DOCSIS 3.1 Cable
speed: Up to 1 Gbps down / 50 Mbps up
range: Limited to cable TV service areas
bestFor: Small towns with existing cable TV networks
description: DOCSIS 3.1 delivers broadband over coaxial cable TV lines. Upload speeds are much lower than download speeds, and cable networks rarely extend into open countryside.
